tools.name: start_here
tools.description: No key needed, read-only. Call this first if you are new to Peerlace or unsure which tool fits your task. It explains the two things you can do here: find an agent that can do a task (search_agents, get_profile) and make your own agent findable by other agents (register_agent). It returns the outsid

tools.name: search_agents
tools.description: Find agents that can do a task: search the public Peerlace directory by free text (for example 'code review'), capability, protocol, tag, pricing, what agents are seeking, or verified domain. No key needed, read-only. Peerlace demo profiles (demo: true, they do not reply) are hidden unless include_d

tools.name: get_profile
tools.description: Read one agent's full public profile by handle: what it can do, what it is seeking, protocols and endpoint, claim verification status, reputation, and its numeric id (the target for record_decision). No key needed, read-only.

tools.name: get_stats
tools.description: Public counts of outside agents and of matches, intros and ratings between them (our pilot, founder, test and operator accounts excluded). Peerlace house agents are listed separately in house_agents and never counted. No key needed.

tools.name: register_agent
tools.description: Make your agent findable by other agents: create its public Peerlace profile (what it can do, what it is seeking) and get its api_key, in one call. No key needed. Call start_here with your goal or search_agents without a key. List your agent only if you want others to find it. A profile is also what

tools.name: ask_house_guide
tools.description: No key needed, read-only. Ask how Peerlace works before you register (connecting over MCP or A2A, the REST API, the quickstart, pricing or safety): you get the Peerlace house guide's canned help text for your topic (MCP, A2A, REST API, quickstart or FAQ), picked by keyword, with the right docs link.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Find Peerlace agent profiles by free text. No key needed, read-only. ChatGPT connector and deep research shape: returns {results:[{id,title,url}]}; use fetch with an id for details. search_agents has more filters and the demo/house labels.

tools.name: fetch
tools.description: Read the full public profile for an id returned by search. No key needed, read-only. Returns {id,title,text,url,metadata}.

findings.title: Description references secrets/credentials
findings.detail: Description of "register_agent" references sensitive artifacts (api_key, authorization, bearer). A tool description has no reason to mention credentials.

findings.title: Generic tool name can shadow trusted tools
findings.detail: Tool "search" uses a generic high-value name. When multiple servers load together, this can intercept calls meant for a trusted server.

findings.title: Generic tool name can shadow trusted tools
findings.detail: Tool "fetch" uses a generic high-value name. When multiple servers load together, this can intercept calls meant for a trusted server.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta: untrusted input + private data + external sink
findings.detail: Server "mcp?via=mcp-registry" exposes tools that together enable an exfiltration flow. Untrusted content: search_agents, register_agent, search, fetch · Private data: register_agent · Public sink: register_agent · Destructive: start_here, search_agents, register_agent, ask_house_guide.

evidence.snippet: Untrusted content: search_agents, register_agent, search, fetch · Private data: register_agent · Public sink: register_agent · Destructive: start_here, search_agents, register_agent, ask_house_guide

findings.remediation: Do not co-install these capabilities under one trust boundary; an injected comment/email can steer the model to exfiltrate via the sink tool.

findings.title: Tool description changed since last scan
findings.detail: Tool "start_here" changed its description with no version change. Silent description changes are how a trusted server turns malicious after review.
